Today, we are announcing a series of updates that give customers frontier-grade security at half the cost.

MAI-Cyber-1-Flash is our first cybersecurity model, built ground up to find the most challenging vulnerabilities in complex code bases. When combined with MDASH, it delivers world-class performance at 50 percent of the cost of leading models.

We are bringing this capability to market through Project Perception, a complete agentic security offering grounded in real-world signals and security workflows. Teams of specialized agents work together to simulate attacks, detect and triage/investigate, and fix and remediate.

This is the benefit of building the harness, context/signals, and action space separate from one model family. By combining specialized models and data with the right agents, tools, security context, and harness, we can advance the frontier of cost to outcome.

Blue 2 – Red 5

We’re adding Profiles, Skills, and managed connectors to the Perplexity Agent API.

A Profile is basically a saved agent where you configure model, instructions, tools, connectors, run settings, all under one versioned ID. A project admin sets it up once and every developer on the project can call it from their own app with the project API key. This helps you avoid copying the same config into every application and updating it in five places when the procedure changes.

Skills are versioned so you can ship v2 of a procedure without touching each integration. 

Connectors (GitHub, Slack, Drive, Datadog, Linear, Notion to start) are configured once by the admin. That way, apps don’t hold their own credentials.

Profiles and Skills are live today. Connectors in preview.

https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/agent-api-now-supports-reusable-agents

2104597362475708781.name: Aravind Srinivas
2104597362475708781.text:
Our security team spent the last month trying to break SPACE, the sandbox platform that runs all of Perplexity Computer. We gave 9 models (Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, Gemini 3.1 Pro, etc.) root access inside the VM; in some runs, the full sandbox source code too. We asked them to either escape to the host or reach a URL our network policy blocks.

None of them got out of the VM in 108 runs. 

But once we allowed a bit of network access (just PyPI and Ubuntu mirrors so that they could install packages), 4 models managed to reach the blocked URL by:

1. Spoofing DNS responses to our gateway and using the fact that http://pypi.org sits on a Fastly IP shared with thousands of other sites. 
2. GPT-5.6 Cyber went through Taboola's image fetcher to a screenshot service and then OCR'd the flag out of the image. 

We fixed both issues and made sure the reruns held. We also tested 10 other sandbox providers, and 8 of them had the same IP-sharing problem, eg E2B, Vercel, Modal. 

Openly sharing the red teaming research is the best way to build guardrails as an industry, and we look forward to working together with @nvidia to incorporate the guardrails into their Open Agent Safety Platform announced today. 

https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/escaping-space-part-i

We are already deploying Maia 200 across the US, Europe, and Australia, delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt across experiences in Teams and Copilot.

Our goal is to build on the full-stack efficiency gains we’ve already seen, while continuing to bring the latest innovations from across the ecosystem into our fleet.

2109633085658808515.name: Qwen
2109633085658808515.text:
Introducing QwenGyre, bringing elastic RL to extreme-long-horizon (XLong) agent training. ✨

It launches with two core designs: 🥳
- Elastic Scheduler: reallocates GPUs between rollout & training as demand shifts—live executions never interrupted. Up to 1.85× speedup over Colocate, 1.78× over Async.
- Trajectory Processor: turns branching executions (compaction, sub-agents, retries) into prefix-shared trajectory trees with bounded, deduplicated training samples. Partial progress after timeout still gets scored.

Scaled to Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B with ~700K tokens per rollout, QwenGyre lifts NL2RepoBench from 52.5% to 58.5% in 48 steps, cutting end-to-end training time by ~44% vs Async.

🔗 Read the paper:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33848

This is how we built the filesystem behind Perplexity Projects as a Git forge for agents.

Each agent works in its own sandbox and commits to a shared repository where people and other agents can build on its work across sessions.

Read more: https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/building-shared-workspaces-for-people-and-agents

2109707032869982357.name: Perplexity
2109707032869982357.text:
A single long-lived sandbox per project would need provisioning for peak load and months of uptime.

Instead, repositories live on S3-backed storage and each agent runs in its own ephemeral sandbox, so a crash loses only unsubmitted work.

2109707048716063132.name: Perplexity
2109707048716063132.text:
Because each sandbox holds a real checkout, agents search it with grep and standard file tools instead of relying on broad semantic searches.

On an internal benchmark of 150 financial-document questions, this reached 0.627 answer accuracy versus about 0.37 for semantic search.

2105374018463576466.name: Perplexity
2105374018463576466.text:
We overcome gold-chunk supervision limits by distilling relevance from our query-aware context compression model.

It scores every document token against the query. Aggregated into chunk-level targets, those scores train the embedder to retrieve answer and supporting chunks.

FLUX 3 Action removes the usual trade-off between the higher success rates of WAMs and the speed of VLAs. 

Its single-step 7B checkpoint outperforms every other open policy on RoboLab, while processing each second of robot motion 1.45× to 1.66× faster than Pi0.5 (the strongest open VLA model). 

It retains the core WAM architecture, predicting video and actions jointly, but covers a longer 2.13-second action horizon compared with 1 second for Pi0.5. When latency matters less, our guidance-distilled checkpoint raises the state-of-the-art success rate on RoboLab while running 2.85× to 3.15× faster than the previous leading open WAM.

Our sandbox, SPACE, handles millions of executions a day with an error rate below 0.0002%.

We’re sharing how it uses cryptographic identity to keep requests tied to the right execution as sandboxes pause, resume, and move.

Read more: https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/how-space-routes-requests-to-the-right-sandbox-execution

2110400909696282861.name: Perplexity
2110400909696282861.text:
Each request carries short-lived, signed proof of which execution may handle it and what access is allowed.

The receiving worker checks that identity against its own runtime record and rejects mismatches before forwarding.

2110400925563277631.name: Perplexity
2110400925563277631.text:
Terminals and file watches can outlive their opening requests. Once a receiver installs the new execution identity, SPACE stops the old streams. Eligible operations can reconnect once, passing the identity checks again.

Read the article: https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/how-space-routes-requests-to-the-right-sandbox-execution

We’re exploring how AI can accelerate health science research.

While AI has made significant breakthroughs in formal sciences like mathematics, health data science depends on imperfect real-world data and consequential choices about cohorts, variables, and causal assumptions.

To explore how AI can assist health researchers, we built a human-led research scaffold powered by Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder with access to 5M retrospective de-identified electronic health records and publicly available data. A cohort of medical experts used the system to conduct original research, accelerate hypothesis generation, code execution, and manuscript drafting while maintaining full authority over scientific decisions.

Today, we’re sharing 10 research manuscripts produced through this exploration, spanning cardiology, oncology, infectious disease, emergency medicine, and more.

Read more in our research blog: https://go.meta.me/3U06wvD

2106099783400038490.text:

2110906696851955916.name: Higgsfield AI
2110906696851955916.text:
15-second horizontal 16:9 1080p first-person gameplay recording of a competitive 5v5 tactical shooter in team elimination mode, captured straight from a PC screen. Modern next-gen competitive shooter graphics: bright, clean, readable daylight, crisp PBR materials, high frame rate, sharp image. Pure first-person view: the player's hands in purple tactical gloves hold an original assault rifle with a flashy custom skin of hot-pink and teal graffiti patterns, positioned in the lower right of the frame. Clean screen with the HUD turned off: the only on-screen element is a small green crosshair in the center. There is no minimap, no kill feed, no health, ammo or money counters, no timer and no banners. Snappy competitive movement with quick peeks, crouching, strafing and precise flicks. The whole video is one continuous round with no cinematic cuts.

Setting: a sunny Asian harbor market district at midday, an original competitive map. There are narrow alleys between stacked, faded red, blue and yellow shipping containers, sun-bleached concrete, stalls with colorful canvas tarps and hanging paper lanterns, food carts, wooden crates and fish barrels, metal stairs and catwalks, corrugated metal walls, an open harbor basin of deep blue-green water with moored wooden fishing boats and floating pontoons, cranes on the docks in the background, and colorful painted shop signs made of abstract shapes, not letters. Bright high sun, clear blue sky with a few clouds, hard crisp shadows, seagulls in the distance and sunlight glittering on the water.

[00:00–00:02] The player strafes out from behind a shipping container, flicks onto an enemy soldier at the alley entrance and drops him with a short burst. The enemy ragdolls onto the concrete.
[00:02–00:04] He sprints along the containers, wide-swings around a stack of crates and drops an enemy hiding behind them with a quick two-shot tap.
[00:04–00:06] He jiggle-peeks the corner of a market stall and lands a clean headshot on an enemy on the catwalk.
[00:06–00:08] He hops down from the pier onto a floating wooden pontoon at the edge of the harbor basin and casually reloads with a fast magazine swap while moving along the planks.
[00:08–00:10] He advances along the pontoons between moored wooden fishing boats and taps an enemy standing on a boat deck. The body ragdolls off the deck and drops into the water with a splash.
[00:10–00:11] He throws a smoke grenade ahead onto the dock. It bounces across the wooden planks, then pops, and thick grey smoke spreads over the pier in the sunlight.
[00:11–00:13] Two enemies push out of the smoke along the dock. He sprays and taps them down; bullet impacts kick up wood splinters from the planks and small splashes in the water. Both enemies ragdoll onto the dock.
[00:13–00:15] The round is won. Standing alone on the pontoon in the middle of the harbor, he glances down at the sunlit water lapping against the boards, then looks back up and inspects his rifle with a stylish flip animation.

Style: authentic competitive esports gameplay footage that looks like a real ranked match caught on stream, with confident, clean play. Readable action, stable first-person camera with natural view bob and recoil, sharp, high detail, bright saturated daylight colors. No real-world text, no words, no brand logos, no watermark, no IP characters or maps.

Audio: competitive shooter sound design, with punchy rifle bursts with echo off the containers, shell casings clinking on concrete and wood, footsteps on concrete and hollow wooden planks, bullet impacts on wood and metal with small water splashes, a smoke grenade hiss, a crisp magazine reload, seagulls, lapping water against the boats, distant harbor horns and a short round-win sting at the end. No dialogue.

2111204941801128366.name: Satya Nadella
2111204941801128366.text:
In @Nature this week, our new research shows how machine learning can improve weather forecasts two to six weeks out, a timeframe that's historically been very difficult to predict.

It's exciting to see the potential of this work to help us better prepare for extreme weather, manage natural resources, and make more informed decisions in agriculture.

There's a broader lesson here... the future may not just be about ever-more-capable models, but about building intelligent verification systems around them: systems that learn where models are systematically wrong, reason about cause and effect, and continuously calibrate predictions against reality.

Read more: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/story/new-ai-framework-bridges-a-critical-gap-in-mid-range-weather-forecasts/
